chapter: The Legends of Jazz and life on the road
title: The Santa Barbara hotel incident with Lionel's band
summary: On Hampton's first tour in 1935 the band was put out of a Santa Barbara hotel after the owner found they were Black.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: I can tell you a little tale about Lionel's band when I
first started with him, when we first went on the road.
Our first job was in Santa Barbara.
This was in California too, not in the south.
This is 1935, my first tour with Lionel.

We got to Santa Barbara early, we had to play two nights there, so we got there in time to go to the jobs. So we didn't look for any place to stay until after we got to work. So we went to work that first night, Gladys was the boss, she was the head of the band, unofficially, and she goes to the big hotel, the Biltmore Hotel, in Santa Barbara.
Anyway, there was a youngster on the desk that night and he didn't care who we were, he said how many are you. He signed us all up and we went to our room and spent the night in bed, except me,

because I had friends in Santa Barbara, so me and my trombone player--we were buddies. The next morning when the boss came in and found out this colored group was in the hotel, he started wringing his hands, 'Oh, what am I going to do; if my regular customers find out they'll all leave; I'll tell you what I'll do, if you all just quietly leave, I won't charge you anything for last night.'
Can you imagine that, in California.
This was 1935 in Santa Barbara, California.
We're not talking behind the Mason-Dixon line.
Not at all. So Gladys talked to Paul Howard--he was kind of the business manager, and they accepted it.
What could they do at that time?
Well, we only spent one night there, it was clean, nice, fine room, a fine bed and everything, for nothing.
So the next night they put us up in a cheap hotel, because we had to stay another night.
That was an incident we had on our first stop on tour with Lionel in 1935, in California.

I'm glad you brought that out because many people think that bigotry and segregation was only in the South, and many of the "northern" cities and states practiced it also, just a little bit more--at times, discreet. The signs weren't up but you could read the lips and you knew that you were not wanted. So I'm told.
